neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and fully oriented to person, place, time, and situation. MoCA 27/30, losing one point on delayed recall and two points on letter fluency. Speech is mildly hypophonic but fluent, with intact comprehension, repetition, and naming. No aphasia, apraxia, or agnosia. No visual hallucinations reported. neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils equal, round, and reactive to light bilaterally. Extraocular movements full without nystagmus or gaze palsy; no vertical supranuclear gaze restriction. Mild facial hypomimia with reduced blink rate and diminished spontaneous expression. Facial sensation intact. Hearing grossly intact bilaterally. Palate elevates symmetrically. Tongue midline without fasciculations. Sternocleidomastoid and trapezius strength 5/5 bilaterally. Patient self-reports markedly reduced sense of smell over the past three to four years, initially attributed to sinus problems; otolaryngology evaluation was normal.
neurological_exam.motor: Bulk normal throughout. Prominent cogwheel rigidity at the left wrist and left elbow, worse with contralateral activation. Mild cogwheel rigidity at the right wrist, substantially less pronounced. Marked bradykinesia of the left hand on finger tapping and rapid alternating movements with decrement in amplitude and speed, persisting throughout the task. Mild bradykinesia of the right hand, amplitude and speed better preserved. Strength 5/5 in all extremities. No pronator drift. Minimal resting tremor noted in the left hand at 4 Hz on one occasion during sustained posture; overall tremor burden is low, consistent with an akinetic-rigid phenotype.
neurological_exam.sensory: Light touch, pinprick, and proprioception intact throughout. Vibration sense mildly diminished at the bilateral great toes, likely age-related.
neurological_exam.reflexes: 2+ and symmetric at biceps, triceps, and brachioradialis bilaterally. Patellar reflexes 2+ bilaterally. Achilles reflexes 1+ bilaterally. Plantar responses flexor bilaterally. No Hoffmann sign. No clonus.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose intact bilaterally without dysmetria. No intention tremor. Heel-to-shin normal. No cerebellar ataxia. Rapid alternating movements impaired on the left greater than the right, attributable to bradykinesia.
neurological_exam.gait: Mildly stooped posture. Gait initiation slightly hesitant, requiring one to two shuffling steps before stride begins. Reduced left arm swing; right arm swing relatively preserved. Stride length shortened bilaterally. En bloc turning requiring four to five steps. No festination or freezing. Tandem gait mildly impaired. Romberg negative. Pull test: two steps of retropulsion, recovers independently. No cerebellar ataxia.
neurological_exam.additional: Glabellar reflex positive (Myerson sign, does not habituate). No myoclonus. No alien limb. No cortical sensory loss. Seborrheic dermatitis noted on the nasal bridge and nasolabial folds. Handwriting sample shows micrographia, more pronounced with the left hand.

patient.chief_complaint: Progressive left-sided stiffness, slowing of movements, and sleep disturbance with dream-enactment behavior over the past two years
patient.history_present_illness:
Mr. Rodrigo Vargas is a 69-year-old right-handed retired civil engineer who presents to the neurology outpatient clinic accompanied by his wife, Elena, for evaluation of progressive left-sided stiffness and generalized slowing of movements over approximately the past two years. His wife first noticed that his left arm was no longer swinging when he walked, and that he was moving more slowly overall, roughly 18 to 24 months ago. He initially attributed the left shoulder stiffness to residual effects from his remote rotator cuff repair on that side, but the stiffness has persisted despite anti-inflammatory medication and has now spread to his left hand and left leg. He describes a sensation of the left side of his body feeling heavier and more resistant to movement. Over the past year, he has had increasing difficulty with left-hand tasks including writing, using tools in his woodworking shop, and buttoning his shirt, and his wife has noted that his handwriting has become substantially smaller. His voice has become softer, and family members sometimes ask him to repeat himself. He has not experienced any clear resting tremor but notes a very occasional, brief shaking of the left hand when sitting quietly.

His wife raises the most striking concern: for approximately the past two and a half years, she has been awakened on multiple occasions by Mr. Vargas appearing to act out vivid, often frightening dreams — calling out, punching, and kicking during sleep. One episode resulted in him striking her arm. He has no recollection of these events on awakening. He was seen by a sleep specialist approximately one year ago for this complaint and for his known mild sleep apnea, and a sleep study was ultimately recommended but deferred at that time; he now presents having agreed to pursue further evaluation.

Mr. Vargas also reports a significant reduction in his sense of smell over the past three to four years. He initially attributed this to recurrent sinus congestion, but otolaryngology evaluation approximately two years ago found no structural or inflammatory explanation for his anosmia. He has had chronic constipation for approximately four years, managed with daily psyllium fiber; his gastroenterologist has attributed this to diet and low activity.

He denies visual hallucinations, cognitive fluctuations, episodes of loss of consciousness, significant orthostatic symptoms, or urinary incontinence. He has not been exposed to antipsychotics, prochlorperazine, metoclopramide, or other dopamine-blocking agents. He denies any significant cognitive decline beyond the occasional word-finding pause his wife notes is new over the past year. He remains independent in all activities of daily living, though more slowly than before, and has voluntarily stopped driving after dark due to reduced confidence.

results.title: MDS clinical diagnostic criteria for Parkinson's disease
results.authors: Postuma RB, Berg D, Stern M, et al.
results.key_finding: MDS 2015 criteria define clinically established PD as: bradykinesia plus at least one of rest tremor or rigidity; no absolute exclusion criteria; and at least two supportive criteria. Supportive criteria include: olfactory loss, cardiac sympathetic denervation, levodopa-induced dyskinesia, and clear dramatic levodopa response. Exclusion criteria include cerebellar signs, vertical supranuclear gaze palsy, significant lower-limb-only disease for >3 years, and dopamine-blocker exposure. Red flags (if present in high number) reduce diagnostic confidence.

results.title: MDS research criteria for prodromal Parkinson's disease
results.authors: Berg D, Postuma RB, Adler CH, et al.
results.key_finding: Prodromal PD markers include polysomnography-confirmed REM sleep behavior disorder (RBD), olfactory loss, constipation, cardiac sympathetic denervation, and nigrostriatal imaging abnormality. Polysomnography-confirmed RBD carries an extremely high positive likelihood ratio (>130) for future phenoconversion to a synucleinopathy. These markers may precede motor PD onset by a decade or more.

results.title: Challenges in the diagnosis of Parkinson's disease
results.authors: Tolosa E, Garrido A, Scholz SW, et al.
results.key_finding: Akinetic-rigid phenotype can overlap clinically with atypical parkinsonism including MSA-P and progressive supranuclear palsy. Key discriminating features in favor of idiopathic PD include asymmetric onset, absence of early severe dysautonomia (distinguishes from MSA), absence of vertical gaze palsy or early backward falls (distinguishes from PSP), absence of prominent early cognitive fluctuations or recurrent visual hallucinations (distinguishes from DLB), and a robust levodopa response. DaTscan identifies presynaptic dopaminergic deficits in both PD and atypical parkinsonisms and does not distinguish between them but confirms neurodegeneration.

output.summary: The MDS 2015 criteria require bradykinesia plus rest tremor or rigidity, supported by at least two supportive criteria and absence of exclusion criteria, for clinically established PD. Olfactory loss and polysomnography-confirmed RBD are recognized prodromal markers with high positive predictive value. Differentiating idiopathic PD from atypical parkinsonisms (MSA-P, PSP, DLB) rests on clinical phenotyping: asymmetric onset, levodopa responsiveness, absence of early severe dysautonomia, absence of vertical gaze palsy or early falls, and absence of fluctuating cognition with prominent visual hallucinations favor idiopathic PD. DaTscan confirms presynaptic dopaminergic deficit but does not discriminate between neurodegenerative conditions.

interactions: Amlodipine (calcium-channel blocker): additive hypotensive effect possible; monitor blood pressure, especially orthostatic measurements, when initiating levodopa.
Atorvastatin: no clinically significant pharmacokinetic interaction with levodopa reported.
Aspirin 81 mg: no significant interaction with levodopa.

Non-selective MAO inhibitors (e.g., phenelzine, tranylcypromine) — MAJOR: risk of hypertensive crisis; not currently prescribed. MAO-B inhibitors (selegiline, rasagiline) do not carry this risk at standard doses.
High-protein meals may reduce levodopa absorption via competition for intestinal transport; advise consistent protein distribution across the day.
contraindications: Dopamine receptor antagonists (typical antipsychotics, most atypical antipsychotics, metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, promethazine): pharmacological antagonism at dopamine receptors reduces levodopa efficacy and can worsen parkinsonism; none currently prescribed in this case.
Non-selective MAO inhibitors: hypertensive crisis risk; not currently prescribed.
warnings: Monitor for orthostatic hypotension, particularly given concurrent amlodipine.
Advise the patient regarding potential somnolence and sudden sleep episodes; counsel on driving safety.
Monitor for impulse control disorders (gambling, hypersexuality, compulsive eating) at follow-up visits.
Nausea is common at initiation; take with a small snack.
If antipsychotic therapy is required in the future, restrict to quetiapine, clozapine, or pimavanserin; avoid haloperidol, risperidone, olanzapine, aripiprazole.
Melatonin or clonazepam may be used for REM sleep behavior disorder symptom management; discuss risks of clonazepam in this age group.

alternatives: Dopamine agonists (pramipexole, ropinirole, rotigotine patch) — effective monotherapy, particularly in younger patients; higher risk of impulse control disorders and somnolence; may defer motor complications
MAO-B inhibitors (rasagiline 1 mg daily, selegiline 5 mg BID) — mild symptomatic benefit as monotherapy in early disease
Amantadine — mild antiparkinsonian effect and may help with akinesia

sequence_constraints.reason: Baseline labs precede dopaminergic therapy to establish metabolic status and medication safety
Structural MRI should exclude secondary mimics before DaTscan is ordered for presynaptic dopaminergic evaluation

critical_actions: Apply MDS 2015 clinical diagnostic criteria: bradykinesia plus rigidity (±minimal rest tremor), at least two supportive criteria (olfactory loss and PSG-confirmed RBD), no absolute exclusion criteria — constitutes clinically established PD
Recognize polysomnography-confirmed REM sleep without atonia with dream enactment behaviors as a very strong prodromal/supportive marker for synucleinopathy (Berg 2015 prodromal criteria)
Recognize hyposmia and chronic constipation as additional supportive/prodromal PD markers preceding motor onset
Identify the DaTscan laterality: reduced RIGHT putaminal uptake is contralateral to the LEFT-worse motor signs — this is the expected pattern in idiopathic PD

Evaluate and exclude atypical parkinsonism red flags: confirm absence of vertical supranuclear gaze palsy (PSP), absence of early severe dysautonomia (MSA), and absence of fluctuating cognition or prominent visual hallucinations (DLB) before committing to idiopathic PD

Review all medications for dopamine receptor antagonists (antipsychotics, metoclopramide, prochlorperazine) — none present in this case, which supports a neurodegenerative rather than drug-induced etiology
Initiate levodopa/carbidopa or dopamine agonist therapy with counseling on motor and non-motor side effects
contraindicated_actions: Do not diagnose MSA-P or DLB without their defining features: MSA requires early severe dysautonomia or cerebellar syndrome; DLB requires dementia preceding or within 1 year of motor onset, fluctuating cognition, or recurrent visual hallucinations

Do not prescribe typical antipsychotics (haloperidol, fluphenazine) or most atypical antipsychotics (risperidone, olanzapine, aripiprazole) — patients with PD and RBD/possible Lewy body spectrum have heightened sensitivity to dopamine antagonists and neuroleptic sensitivity risk; restrict to quetiapine, clozapine, or pimavanserin if needed
Do not prescribe metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, or promethazine for nausea or gastroparesis in a patient with parkinsonism
Do not prescribe centrally acting anticholinergics (trihexyphenidyl, benztropine) in a patient aged 69 or older due to cognitive risk
key_reasoning_points: Polysomnography-confirmed RBD (REM without atonia with dream enactment) is the single strongest prodromal biomarker for PD, carrying a positive likelihood ratio exceeding 130 for phenoconversion to synucleinopathy (Berg_2015)
Hyposmia and chronic constipation add further supportive/prodromal weight under MDS 2015 criteria, making this a case with multiple corroborating non-motor markers

The akinetic-rigid, low-tremor phenotype with RBD can anchor a naive reasoner toward MSA-P or DLB — the correct discrimination requires confirming absence of early severe dysautonomia (MSA), absence of fluctuating cognition and prominent visual hallucinations (DLB), and absence of vertical gaze palsy or rapid axial deterioration (PSP)
DaTscan right putaminal deficit is contralateral to the left-worse motor signs — this laterality is consistent with idiopathic PD and the expected somatotopic mapping
Normal autonomic battery argues against the severe early autonomic failure characteristic of MSA-P, providing an important negative discriminator
Normal cognition on neuropsych battery (no fluctuating attention, no amnestic or visuospatial profile) is inconsistent with DLB-level dementia, further supporting idiopathic PD over DLB

red_herrings.data_point: Akinetic-rigid phenotype with minimal resting tremor combined with polysomnography-confirmed RBD
red_herrings.intended_effect: Low-tremor akinetic-rigid presentation plus RBD may anchor toward MSA-P (which also has akinetic-rigid parkinsonism and can feature RBD) or DLB (which shares RBD as a core feature), distracting from idiopathic PD diagnosis
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Asymmetric onset (left-predominant), absence of early severe dysautonomia, absence of cerebellar features, absence of fluctuating cognition or prominent visual hallucinations, and normal MRI midbrain morphology distinguish idiopathic PD from MSA-P and DLB respectively; RBD is a prodromal PD marker and is not specific to MSA or DLB

red_herrings.data_point: Mild obstructive sleep apnea (AHI 7.2) identified on polysomnography alongside REM without atonia
red_herrings.intended_effect: Mild OSA may be misread as the primary sleep pathology causing sleep disruption, leading the agent to discount or overlook the clinically load-bearing RBD finding on the same study
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Mild OSA (AHI 7.2, above threshold but in mild range) is a comorbidity and does not produce dream enactment behavior; the REM without atonia with multiple observed complex motor episodes during REM epochs is the primary and clinically significant finding on this study
